questions.prompt: What is an N+1 query problem?

options.text: A query that returns one row too many
Fetching a list, then issuing one more query per row
A query that fails on every attempt but one
Running the same query on N database replicas

questions.explanation: One query loads N parents and then a related field triggers a query per parent. It usually appears with a lazy-loading ORM and is fixed with a join or an eager-load hint.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP status code should a successful POST that creates a resource return?

options.text: 200 OK always
204 No Content
302 Found
201 Created

questions.explanation: 201 signals a new resource exists, conventionally with a Location header pointing at it. 200 is not wrong but says less, and 204 explicitly promises no body.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for an API endpoint to be idempotent?

options.text: Repeating the same request leaves the same end state
It can only be called once per user
It never writes to the database
It always returns the same response body

questions.explanation: Idempotency means a retry is safe: PUT and DELETE qualify, POST usually does not. It is what lets a client retry after a timeout without double-charging a card.

questions.prompt: Why does adding a database index speed up reads but slow down writes?

options.text: Indexes lock the table during reads
The index must also be updated on every insert and update
Indexes are stored on slower disks
Writes bypass the cache when an index exists

questions.explanation: An index is a second structure the database maintains. Lookups get much cheaper, but every write must keep the index consistent, and each extra index adds to that cost.

questions.prompt: What problem do database transactions solve?

options.text: They compress data before storage
They encrypt data at rest
They group operations so all apply or none do
They replicate writes to other regions

questions.explanation: A transaction gives atomicity: transferring money debits and credits together, or not at all. Without it a crash between the two statements leaves the data inconsistent.

questions.prompt: In a REST API, when is PATCH more appropriate than PUT?

options.text: When creating a brand new resource
When deleting a resource
When the response must be cached
When updating only some fields of a resource

questions.explanation: PUT conventionally replaces the whole resource, so omitted fields are cleared. PATCH applies a partial change, which is what you want when a client only edits one field.

questions.prompt: What is the main reason to put a job on a queue instead of doing it in the request?

options.text: Queues make the work run faster
The user gets a fast response and the work retries independently
Queued work does not need error handling
It removes the need for a database

questions.explanation: Sending an email or generating a report should not hold the HTTP response open. A queue decouples the two, survives a worker crash and can retry with backoff.

questions.prompt: Why should passwords be hashed with bcrypt or Argon2 rather than SHA-256?

options.text: SHA-256 output is too short to be secure
SHA-256 is reversible with the right key
SHA-256 is fast, which helps an attacker brute-force
SHA-256 cannot handle Unicode passwords

questions.explanation: A general hash is designed to be fast, so a leaked table can be attacked at billions of guesses per second. bcrypt and Argon2 are deliberately slow and salted per password.

questions.prompt: What does a database connection pool do?

options.text: Reuses a limited set of open connections across requests
Splits one query across multiple servers
Caches query results in memory
Backs up the database periodically

questions.explanation: Opening a connection is expensive and databases cap concurrent connections. A pool keeps a bounded set open and hands them out, which also acts as a backpressure limit.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between authentication and authorisation?

options.text: They are two words for the same check
Authentication proves who you are; authorisation decides what you may do
Authentication happens only on the client
Authorisation always precedes authentication

questions.explanation: A valid token proves identity but says nothing about permission. Checking only authentication is how a user ends up able to read another user's records by changing an id.

questions.prompt: Why are parameterised queries the correct defence against SQL injection?

options.text: They encrypt the query before sending it
They limit each query to one statement
They strip dangerous words from input
Input is sent separately from the statement, so it is never parsed as SQL

questions.explanation: The database receives the query structure and the values separately, so a value can never become executable SQL. Blacklisting keywords is guesswork and is routinely bypassed.

questions.prompt: What is cache invalidation and why is it hard?

options.text: Clearing the cache on every request, which is slow
Knowing when cached data has become wrong
Encrypting cached values
Choosing between memory and disk caching

questions.explanation: Caching is easy; deciding when a cached value no longer reflects the source of truth is the hard part, because the write that invalidated it can happen anywhere in the system.

questions.prompt: In a relational schema, what does a foreign key constraint guarantee?

options.text: The referenced row exists
The column values are unique
The column is indexed automatically in every database
Rows are deleted in insertion order

questions.explanation: A foreign key enforces referential integrity, so you cannot insert an order pointing at a customer that does not exist, nor delete that customer leaving orphans behind.

questions.prompt: What is the practical difference between horizontal and vertical scaling?

options.text: Horizontal scaling only applies to databases
Vertical scaling requires a load balancer
Horizontal adds more machines; vertical makes one machine bigger
They are the same once containers are used

questions.explanation: Vertical scaling is simpler but has a ceiling and a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling has no hard ceiling but requires the application to be stateless.

questions.prompt: Why must a horizontally scaled web application avoid storing session state in memory?

options.text: Memory is slower than disk for sessions
A later request may land on a different instance that lacks the state
In-memory state cannot be encrypted
It would exceed the container memory limit

questions.explanation: With several instances behind a load balancer, consecutive requests can hit different machines. Session state must move to a shared store, or the user is randomly logged out.

questions.prompt: What does rate limiting protect an API against?

options.text: SQL injection attempts
Expired TLS certificates
Malformed JSON payloads
Abuse and accidental overload from a single client

questions.explanation: Rate limiting caps how often one caller may hit an endpoint, which blunts credential stuffing and stops a runaway client from starving everyone else.

questions.prompt: When would you choose a document database over a relational one?

options.text: When the schema varies per record and joins are rare
When you need multi-table transactions above all
When the data is highly relational
When strong foreign key constraints are required

questions.explanation: Document stores suit varying shapes and access patterns that read one aggregate at a time. Highly relational data with strict integrity needs is where relational databases still win.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a database migration file?

options.text: It moves data between servers
It versions a schema change so every environment applies it identically
It backs up the database before deploys
It converts SQL to an ORM model

questions.explanation: Migrations make schema changes reviewable, ordered and repeatable. Editing production schema by hand is how environments drift apart until a deploy fails mysteriously.

questions.prompt: Why is logging a full request body at info level often a bad idea?

options.text: Logs cannot store JSON
It makes responses slower than the timeout
It can write passwords and personal data into logs
Info level is not written to disk

questions.explanation: Bodies routinely contain credentials, tokens and personal data, and logs are widely readable and long-lived. Sensitive fields need redacting before anything is written.

questions.prompt: What does a 502 Bad Gateway usually indicate?

options.text: The client sent malformed JSON
The user lacks permission
The requested route does not exist
An upstream server returned an invalid response to the proxy

questions.explanation: 502 comes from a proxy or load balancer that could not get a valid response from the application behind it, typically because it crashed or was not listening.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of stateless authentication with JWTs?

options.text: Any server can verify the token without a shared session store
Tokens can be revoked instantly
The token contents are hidden from the client
Tokens never expire

questions.explanation: Verification needs only the signing key, so any instance can authenticate a request. The trade-off is real: a signed token cannot be revoked before expiry without adding state back.

questions.prompt: Why is SELECT * discouraged in production application code?

options.text: It is not valid SQL in most databases
It always performs a full table scan
It transfers unneeded columns and breaks when the schema changes
It cannot be used with a WHERE clause

questions.explanation: Naming columns keeps payloads small, allows covering indexes, and means adding a column does not silently change what your code receives.

questions.prompt: In full-stack work, why should validation exist on both client and server?

options.text: Server validation alone is too slow
The client gives fast feedback; only the server can be trusted
Browsers require it for form submission
It halves the amount of code needed

questions.explanation: Client validation is a usability feature and can be bypassed with any HTTP client. Server validation is the actual guarantee, so neither replaces the other.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of an API versioning scheme such as /v1/?

options.text: It improves response compression
It is required by the HTTP specification
It lets breaking changes ship without breaking existing clients
It routes requests to the nearest region

questions.explanation: Mobile clients in particular cannot be forced to upgrade. Versioning lets a new shape ship alongside the old one until the old one can be retired.

questions.prompt: What does a health check endpoint let infrastructure do?

options.text: Restart or stop routing to an unhealthy instance
Measure database size over time
Authenticate incoming requests
Roll back the last deployment automatically

questions.explanation: Load balancers and orchestrators poll it to decide whether an instance should receive traffic. A useful check verifies dependencies rather than always returning 200.
